questions.question: Explain why the law 'add exponents when multiplying' works, starting from what an exponent actually means.
questions.expected_answer: An exponent counts repeated multiplication: x³ is three x's multiplied and x² is two x's. Multiplying them strings five x's together, which is x⁵ — so the exponents add. Each law is a consequence of counting factors, not an arbitrary rule.

questions.question: Describe the strategy for solving an exponential equation like 3^(x+1) = 27, and what you would do if the right-hand side were 1 or 1/27 instead.
questions.expected_answer: Express both sides as powers of the same base, then equate exponents: 27 = 3³ gives x + 1 = 3, so x = 2. If the right side were 1, write it as 3⁰ (x = −1); if 1/27, write it as 3⁻³ (x = −4). The base-matching move is identical in every variation.

questions.question: In your own words, explain why a negative exponent is a 'position instruction, not a sign', using 4x⁻² as your example.
questions.expected_answer: The negative exponent tells the power to move across the fraction line, not to become negative: x⁻² means 1/x², so 4x⁻² is 4/x² — a positive quantity for any nonzero x. Writing −4x² or −4/x² confuses relocation with negation.
